title: Fishing nets

names.gloss: tree bark which can be used as vine. it was used to make fishnets, which were dragged through the water in the dry season when the water goes down.
names.note: Roth recorded warur (his spelling) at Bloomfield as the string made from fig-tree bark.

names.gloss: dilly bag; the tree bark used to make into strips and weave fishing nets and dilly bags; spider web; placenta

identification.basis: The dictionary gives makarr 'fish net', and defines warrur and ngunyin as the bark used to make fishing nets. Roth's Bloomfield vocabulary, as catalogued by Khan, gives warur or tchul-bal for string made from fig bark, and ngon-yan for the netted bags made from it. Note that Roth (1901) wrote that fish-nets were not used on the Bloomfield; see Description.

summary: A **[makarr](word:makarr)** is a fish net [ref:hershberger1982]. The dictionary records nets made of **[warrur](word:warrur)** bark, 'dragged through the water in the dry season when the water goes down' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth, writing in 1901, thought fish-nets were not used on the Bloomfield, the Endeavour or at Cape Bedford [ref:roth1901]. Yet he collected a two-person oval-frame net on the Bloomfield in 1898, a type made around the Laura [ref:khan1993]. Bloomfield people also got fishing nets in trade from the Laura [ref:roth1910b14]. Inland, on the Palmer and at the Laura, nets on oval frames of [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane) were swept through the water by two people while others drove the fish towards them [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
**[Makarr](word:makarr)** is 'fish net'. **[Warrur](word:warrur)** is 'tree bark which can be used as vine. It was used to make fishnets, which were dragged through the water in the dry season when the water goes down.' **[Ngunyin](word:ngunyin)** means a [dilly bag](entry:dilly-bags), 'the tree bark used to make into strips and weave fishing nets and dilly bags', a spider web, and the placenta [ref:hershberger1982].

Roth's Bloomfield vocabulary fills in the fibre. Khan's catalogue of his collection records that the Bloomfield people called their netted [string](entry:string-and-twine) bags *ngon-yan*. The string, spun from the bark of the fig tree, was called *warur* or *tchul-bal* (Roth's spellings) [ref:khan1993]. Anderson likewise describes the men's bag, the **[ngunyin](word:ngunyin)**, as made of *Ficus* fibre twine [ref:anderson1996]. So the warrur of the nets is probably fig-bark string; see [fig](entry:fig).

At Cooktown, Roth was told that the Guugu Yimithirr word for a net was *magar*, 'i.e. a cobweb' [ref:roth1901]. That sounds close to Kuku Yalanji **[makarr](word:makarr)**, and the Kuku Yalanji **[ngunyin](word:ngunyin)** also joins net-bark and spider web.

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
**Two records that disagree.** Roth wrote in 1901 that 'fish-nets are not employed at Cape Bedford, on the Bloomfield, or on the Endeavour River'. He added that the nearest people who used them were at the Laura, Princess Charlotte Bay and Cape Grafton [ref:roth1901]. Anderson's account of Bloomfield fishing likewise lists [spears](entry:spear-and-woomera), [lines](entry:hooks-and-lines) and [poisons](entry:fish-poisoning), not nets [ref:anderson1996]. Yet:

- Roth collected a **non-folding oval-frame fishing net on the Bloomfield in 1898** (Australian Museum E.14959). It is 137 × 45 cm, woven in loose hour-glass looping with loops 9 cm long; the frame is missing. The museum's 1905 register says 'made at the Laura or Deighton' [ref:khan1993].
- Roth recorded that Bloomfield and Endeavour River people took red [ochre](entry:red-ochre), white clay and [grass-tree](entry:grass-tree) spears up towards the Laura. In return they received [melo](entry:bailer-shells) shells, shell necklaces, [stingray](entry:stingrays) spears and **fishing-nets** [ref:roth1910b14] [ref:anderson1996].
- The 1982 dictionary has **[makarr](word:makarr)** and the warrur nets dragged in the [dry season](entry:seasons) [ref:hershberger1982].

Nets were known and used, even if, in Roth's day, many were traded in rather than made on the coast.

**Kinds of net in the region** [ref:roth1901]:

- **Non-folding oval-frame nets**, with mesh in hour-glass looping, are found only on Cape York Peninsula: on the Morehead, Musgrave, Normanby, Laura, Palmer, Embley, Pennefather and Batavia Rivers. The Koko-yellanji (Roth's spelling) of the Laura called this net *jikan-ikan*.
- **Folding 'purse' nets** on oval frames, with European-style netting-stitch mesh, run from Princess Charlotte Bay south to Hinchinbrook Island and west to the Gulf. They fold shut like a purse when a fish is in. On the lower Tully the net is called *mokaro*.
- **Scoops**: on the lower Tully, women dipped their everyday [lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) dilly-bags into the stream to catch fry swimming upstream in floods. Men scooped prawns at the river mouth in long split-cane baskets. See [dilly bags](entry:dilly-bags) and [cherabin](entry:cherabin).

sections.heading: Where and when
sections.body:
The dictionary places warrur netting in **the dry season, 'when the water goes down'** [ref:hershberger1982]. As the creeks shrink, the fish are crowded into shallow pools where a net can sweep them. On the lower Tully, folding nets were also set in narrow channels in flood time [ref:roth1901].

**The upper Mitchell.** The nearest recorded nets are the two-person nets of the Palmer River and the Laura [ref:roth1901]. Only about 4% of the Mitchell catchment's rain falls between May and October [ref:griffith2021], so the late dry is when its side creeks and lagoons shrink to pools.

sections.heading: What they caught
sections.body: Roth names few species. Folding nets set with wings in flood time on the Tully were 'especially for "rock cod"', and the tiny fry scooped in [dilly-bags](entry:dilly-bags) were wrapped in [wild-ginger](entry:wild-ginger) leaves and baked [ref:roth1901]. A dry-season sweep of a waterhole on the Mitchell would take fish such as [black bream](entry:black-bream), [catfish](entry:catfish) and [cherabin](entry:cherabin).

sections.heading: How nets were made and used
sections.body:
**Making the twine** [ref:khan1993] [ref:roth1901-string]:

1. Strip the bark: at Bloomfield, [fig](entry:fig) bark (*warur*). On the Palmer, the string was made from the wattle *Acacia leptocarpa* [ref:roth1901]. Further north it came from *Acacia latifolia* or the cabbage-tree palm.
2. For *Acacia latifolia*, soak the inner bark all morning, when it turns red. Then dry it in the sun and split it into shreds.
3. Roll each shred forwards on your outer thigh to make a strand. Fold it in two and roll it under pressure, forwards and then sharply back, so the two halves twist into two-ply twine. Join new shreds as you go. See [string and twine](entry:string-and-twine).

**Looping the mesh** [ref:khan1993] [ref:roth1901-string]:

4. Start with one straight base strand. On the Bloomfield bags it was tied between two sticks set in the ground.
5. Work one continuous strand in hour-glass (double-loop) looping along it, row after row. For a net the looping is kept very loose. On the Bloomfield net the loops are 9 cm long.

**The frame (Princess Charlotte Bay hinterland)** [ref:roth1901]:

6. Make an oval of [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane) in two or three pieces, firmly lashed together. It is usually about 2½ feet wide and 5 feet long (about 75 cm × 1.5 m), often bigger.
7. Lash the net to it.

**Fishing with a two-person net (Palmer River and Princess Charlotte Bay)** [ref:roth1901]:

8. Two people carry the net upright through the water.
9. Friends walk ahead as beaters, driving the fish towards it.
10. Lift the net as soon as a fish is in.

**A folding net on the lower Tully (Mallanpara country)** [ref:roth1901]: fix the net open between two stakes in a narrow channel, where the current holds it open. When the beaters drive a fish close, the person watching from the bank or a snag dives in and shuts it.

The dictionary records that warrur nets were dragged, but not how many people pulled them or how the catch was landed [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body: A net that snags underwater can trap a swimmer, so keep a knife handy and never tie a net to yourself. Shrinking dry-season waterholes are where crocodiles shelter too; see [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile).

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
**Recreational rules (Queensland fresh waters).** The only nets allowed are **scoop or dip nets**, no bigger than 1 m in any dimension, with a handle up to 2.5 m long and mesh no bigger than 25 mm, plus landing nets for line-caught fish. Cast nets, seine nets, bait nets and drum nets are banned in fresh waters [ref:qld-gear]. A traditional oval-frame net, at 1.5 m long, is too big to count as a scoop net.

**Aboriginal tradition and native title.** Queensland's *Fisheries Act 1994* gives an Aboriginal person acting under Aboriginal tradition a defence for fishing with recreational gear, or with traditional fish traps of stone or organic material [ref:qld-fishact] [ref:qld-fishreg]. A traditional drag net is neither. Section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* lifts licence and permit requirements for native title holders fishing for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs [ref:alrc]. Western Yalanji native title includes rights to fish [ref:brady2013]. How s 211 meets an outright gear ban has not been settled in the sources found, so native title holders should ask their prescribed body corporate. Everyone else should ask the Traditional Owners, and the station at [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters).

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: **[Karra](word:karra)** 'rope, cord, string'; **[ngurran](word:ngurran)** 'rope, also dilly bag made from rope'; **[murnil](word:murnil)** 'twist, stir'; **[kajal](word:kajal)** 'to tie'; **[marral](word:marral)** 'dry'; **[kuyu](word:kuyu)** 'fish' [ref:hershberger1982].
